name: Lena Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so you can give me your public line and your private view. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Lena, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company that makes school-meal ordering software. I have a bachelor’s degree, and I spend mornings checking order failures, then fix code and review the lunch totals with the support team. I’m competent but not the person who can solve every strange fault alone. I use AI every day to draft tests and find old code, then check the allergy flags myself. A missed meal matters more than a clever demo.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household riding on this work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Ruth, works as a home-care aide, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My pay is low for a developer, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few other developer jobs nearby. One missed shift or a car repair can undo our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau is close to the tools we already use: quick test drafts, with people checking the meals. I would still insist on a human review of allergy changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be relieved about my job but not about the mortgage. The school contract is small, my pay is low, and a late payment would hurt before AI ever does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using AI for test drafts and check each allergy flag against the school’s order record. I’d put 30 into a bill buffer after payday if Ruth’s shifts hold. In the first year I’d ask my manager for a pay review tied to the last two safe releases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, although the work itself looks steady. A calm AI story would not make our car cheaper to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes first in the home budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Ruth we can keep the children’s lunches paid but postpone the new kitchen shelves. If the car needs work for her visits, the shelves wait longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to a pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show my manager the two releases with no allergy corrections and the support tickets they avoided. I would ask for a date, not count on a raise.

say: I see **AI Plateau** as quick drafts that still need meal checks.
I would insist on **human allergy review** before school orders go out.
think: I expect my **job** to stay but worry about the mortgage.
My **low pay** and small school contract leave little room for a late payment.
do: **Keep** drafting tests with AI and checking allergy flags against school records.
**Save** 30 after payday if Ruth’s care shifts hold.
**Request** a pay review with two safe releases; postpone kitchen shelves while protecting lunches and Ruth’s car.
feel: **Anxious** about bills despite expected work stability.
S0.quote: A calm AI story would not make our car cheaper to fix.
fieldNote: Her **baseline money strain** remains in AI Plateau despite daily AI use and steady technical work.
The **30 transfer** depends on Ruth’s shifts; any raise remains a request, not guaranteed income.
The **shelf purchase** waits behind the children’s lunches and Ruth’s work car.

steps.text: Keep drafting meal tests with AI and checking allergy flags
Save 30 after payday if Ruth’s care shifts hold
Postpone new kitchen shelves to protect lunches and Ruth’s car repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let AI write more code, answer parents and place meal orders. I would ask for paid time to test allergy errors before anyone cuts reviewers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think our three-person team may become two, and I could be the one who leaves. Ruth’s care visits may stay, but one wage cannot cover our mortgage for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d run the assistant against twenty old allergy mistakes and record every miss. I’d ask for paid time to learn the school’s food rules from our support lead; if denied, I’d use the free guide after the children are asleep. If management announces a reviewer cut in the first year, I’d join the workplace union meeting and bring the error list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I use AI gladly, but a smaller meal-software team could still cost me my paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children if your hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children we may skip the weekend trip, not that the house is gone. I would talk to Ruth about the mortgage numbers after they are asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management to sign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell management which allergy cases the assistant missed and ask them to sign the final review rule. If they refuse paid learning time, I could manage one free evening, not a new degree.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, parent replies and meal orders.
I would seek **paid allergy testing** before reviewer jobs are cut.
think: I expect our **three-person team** could shrink, possibly removing my role.
I cannot cover the **mortgage** for long on Ruth’s wage alone.
do: **Test** AI against twenty old allergy mistakes this month.
**Study** food rules in paid time, or use the free guide if refused.
**Attend** the union meeting if management announces a reviewer cut.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely lost pay despite using AI daily.
S1.quote: I use AI gladly, but a smaller meal-software team could still cost me my paycheck.
fieldNote: Her **technical openness** does not protect her from a probable three-to-two team cut.
Her **learning time** requires company pay or one free evening, and union action follows an announced cut.

steps.text: Test AI against twenty old school allergy mistakes
Learn school food rules in paid time or from free guide if refused
Attend workplace union meeting if reviewer cut is announced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 can do our coding and meal planning by 2028. Hands-on robots arrive around 2031; Ruth’s home-care visits may have more time than my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer job to disappear and our mortgage to rest on Ruth’s visits. Less than one month saved will not bridge a long search, and there are few nearby coding jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the mortgage lender now what a hardship arrangement needs and gather our payment records. I’d stop the weekend trip and keep money for food and Ruth’s car. In the first year after 2028, if I am laid off, I’d apply for any real local openings and for income help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and close to losing sleep. I can make calls, but I cannot turn a thin account into a cushion in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you call the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call before a missed mortgage payment and ask for the terms in writing. I would not assume the lender will reduce a bill just because I explain the situation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help with the children during a search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Ruth the children need routines even if I lose work. I would ask my sister to watch them for interviews only if her own shifts allow.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach meal code before hands-on robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Ruth’s **care visits** may change later than my desk work.
think: I expect my **developer income** to disappear.
Our **thin savings** and few nearby jobs cannot bridge a long search.
do: **Ask** the lender now about hardship terms before missing payment.
**Cancel** the weekend trip while protecting food and work transport.
**Apply** for actual local openings and eligible income help if laid off after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely income loss and almost no savings runway.
S2.quote: I cannot turn a thin account into a cushion in two years.
fieldNote: She sees the **2028 desk-work shock** before hands-on robots around 2031 may affect Ruth.
The **lender inquiry** is not relief; public help and sister’s childcare depend on eligibility and shifts.

steps.text: Cancel weekend trip and preserve food and car money
Apply for actual local openings if laid off after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if laid off after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to plan for our school-meal code changing. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2034, later than the code shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect a smaller developer team, but the warning lets me learn more about school operations while wages continue. I do not know if those operations jobs will survive full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one paid afternoon a month with the school support team learning how missing meals are corrected. I’d use the free food-safety course they recommend and keep records of cases I helped solve. In the first year after 2031, if my coding role ends, I’d apply for actual school support openings that still pay enough for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years gives me a path to test. The mortgage still needs a paycheck every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show you can do support work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take two case records to an interview and explain what went wrong in ordinary words. I would not pay for a certificate unless a real opening required it and we could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the family housing plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I would keep our present home and set aside 30 after payday when her visits are steady. I would not plan a move without a job offer and a clear housing cost.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as warning to prepare for changed meal code.
I know **2034 robots** arrive later than thinking AI for my work.
think: I expect a **smaller coding team** even with five years to prepare.
I cannot assume **school support** survives full thinking AI.
do: **Learn** missing-meal corrections in one paid support afternoon monthly.
**Complete** a free food-safety course, record cases and set aside 30 after payday when Ruth’s visits are steady.
**Apply** for actual mortgage-paying support openings if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about ongoing mortgage payments despite a usable warning period.
S3.quote: The mortgage still needs a paycheck every month.
fieldNote: She uses **paid support time** and a free course rather than spending scarce cash on speculative certificates.
A **support move** depends on real openings and enough pay; home plans remain tied to actual offers.
The **30 deposit** depends on Ruth’s visits, while the family keeps its present home.

steps.text: Learn missing-meal corrections monthly and complete free food-safety course
Apply for real school support jobs paying the mortgage if coding ends
Set aside 30 after payday only when Ruth’s care visits are steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to build safer meal software and plan our work. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could improve my role over ten years, but this month’s low pay still strains us. AGI by 2036 does not cover our car repair or mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining meal orders and check AI tests against allergy records each week. I’d ask for a pay review this year using the safe-release record, and save 30 after payday only when Ruth’s shifts hold. In the first year after 2036, if my coding job ends, I’d search for real offers and compare pay before moving the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money now, but able to plan for later technical change. I will not pretend the decade fixes our current bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pay review brings no raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager for a written pay-review date and show the allergy incidents we prevented. If the raise is refused, our savings target stays small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I would keep the children in their current school unless a real job pays enough to cover a move. I would not gamble their routine on a forecast.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to build safer meal software.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I can grow **technical skills** over a decade while wages continue, if my job lasts.
I still face **low pay** and mortgage pressure now, long before the 2036 change.
do: **Keep** checking meal-code changes against allergy records weekly.
**Request** a safe-release pay review and save 30 after payday only when Ruth’s shifts hold.
**Search** for real offers and compare pay before moving the family if coding ends after 2036.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills despite longer preparation time.
S4.quote: AGI by 2036 does not cover our car repair or mortgage payment.
fieldNote: Her **baseline income strain** remains despite an extra decade to adapt.
A **pay review** is conditional and her 30 savings transfer depends on Ruth’s work schedule.

steps.text: Keep checking weekly meal-code changes against school allergy records
Save 30 after payday only when Ruth’s care shifts hold
Search for real offers and compare pay before moving if coding ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our mortgage has no gap month and my code work could end fast. Written notice, income help we qualify for and paid time to learn school operations would help. I would still need someone to check that children with allergies get the right meal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask which child goes without lunch when an automatic order looks correct but is wrong. A wrong school-meal order has a child’s name on it, even if the code has none.

headlineQuote: A wrong school-meal order has a child’s name on it, even if the code has none.
portrait: Lena is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, average skill and daily AI use on school-meal software.
Her **low pay**, mortgage, two children and savings under one month create anxiety even under AI Plateau.
She expects **team cuts** under Steady Disruption despite using AI well; Ruth’s care work faces robots later.
She seeks **paid learning**, conditional income help and actual school support vacancies while protecting food and work transport.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her code income before she can build even one month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, eligible income help and paid time to learn school operations would help.
